title: A World Model of Life: Biohub's Alex Rives on Virtual Cells, Measurement, & the $1.8B Data Push
guest: Alex Rives（Biohub 科学负责人，前 ESM 蛋白语言模型负责人）
summary: Biohub 要构建「生命的预测性世界模型」：在扩大至 18 亿美元的虚拟生物学计划（合作方含美国能源部、NIH、Google DeepMind、Meta）支持下绘制数千亿细胞的情境化图谱；为何当下 AI 架构还做不出真正的虚拟细胞、激光相位板等测量技术突破的重要性、跨尺度与跨模式生物学习，以及五年内实现「信息层面细胞模型」、让医学从传统药物走向可编程干预的路线。

## 这期在聊什么

Alex Rives（前 EvolutionaryScale / ESM 蛋白语言模型核心人物，现 Biohub 科学侧负责人）谈一个听起来像科幻、实际在砸数据与测量的议程：**生命的预测性世界模型**。在扩大至约 **18 亿美元**量级的虚拟生物学计划支持下（合作方叙述涵盖能源部、NIH、DeepMind、Meta 等），目标是绘制海量细胞的情境化图谱，并追问：当下 AI 架构为何还做不出真正的「虚拟细胞」、测量技术（如激光相位板）为何与模型同等重要、五年尺度上「信息层面细胞模型」如何让医学从传统药物走向更可编程的干预。

## 核心论点

### 1. 宏大使命要落到「什么可预测」

Rives 自称偏实践：先问什么在近期可被数据与测量支撑，而不是先写哲学定义。虚拟细胞不是再做一个会聊天的生物百科，而是要对扰动与状态转移给出可检验预测。

### 2. 数据规模与情境化图谱

节目强调海量细胞、多情境测量——没有情境的组学表型很难支撑「世界模型」。18 亿级计划的叙事重点是：**把生物学变成可学习的大规模结构化数据问题**，同时承认现有模型距离「真正虚拟细胞」仍远。

### 3. 测量与模型同样是瓶颈

类比自动驾驶的传感器辩论：只堆模型不够，感知与测量分辨率决定你能学到什么。激光相位板等技术被当作打开新数据分布的钥匙——这提醒 AI for Science 听众：算法叙事常低估仪器与实验通量。

### 4. 跨尺度、模式生物与人类数据

生物学原则可能跨生物共享，但模式生物到人的迁移从来不是免费的。健康记录与语言数据的价值被谨慎讨论：语言强，但能否替代精细分子测量，嘉宾并不装确定。

### 5. 五年愿景：信息层细胞模型与可编程干预

路线图语气是「有雄心、有条件」：先在信息层面建立可用的细胞模型，再谈医学干预形态变化。听众应把时间表当研究纲领，而非获批疗法承诺。

## 要点

- AI for Science 的瓶颈经常是测量与实验设计，不只是参数量。
- 「虚拟细胞」要用预测任务定义，避免幻灯片概念。
- 与蛋白语言模型经验对照：表示学习强，不等于系统级仿真已成。

## 听法建议

非生物背景听众可先抓「测量=传感器」「虚拟细胞=可检验预测」两个类比，再听合作网络与资金叙事。涉及具体机构名单、金额与技术专名，请以 Biohub 与原片为准。

## 与谁对照

可与 Latent Space 科学向、库内 Biohub 相关条目连读；也可和具身「世界模型」讨论对照：都是预测性模型，但数据生成成本与伦理约束完全不同。

# 详细解读：生命世界模型是数据与测量的联合工程

## 一、为何这期对 AI for Science 重要

多数「AI+生物」播客停在蛋白折叠成功叙事。Rives 把问题升级到系统：细胞状态、扰动、跨尺度。这迫使听众承认——表示学习的胜利不等于虚拟生命已可商业化部署。

## 二、用预测任务定义「虚拟细胞」

好定义应回答：给定干预，下一状态分布是什么？哪些观测足够识别状态？失败时如何证伪模型？没有这些，虚拟细胞只是品牌词。

## 三、18 亿叙事的正确读法

大资金是必要非充分条件。解读重点应放在：数据治理、实验通量、跨机构标准、负责任发布。金额本身不是科学里程碑。

## 四、测量技术作为一等公民

相位板等突破提醒：AI 团队若只招算法、不理解光与样本制备，会训在错误分布上。组织上应让实验物理/光学与 ML 共享 OKR。

## 五、从药物到可编程干预的修辞边界

这是方向性愿景。监管、制造、临床试验仍是独立长链。精读/解读不得把研究愿景写成医疗承诺。

## 六、给投资者与实验室的清单

问清：主预测任务是什么；测量瓶颈是什么；模式生物到人的迁移计划；数据开放与安全边界；五年成功的可观测指标（非融资指标）。

## 七、材料边界

依据 Cognitive Revolution 转写与节目简介；合作方与金额以官方披露为准。自动转写专名需人工核。

## 八、与 ESM 经验的连续与断裂

蛋白 LM 证明序列表示可学；细胞世界模型需要更多状态与干预数据。连续的是表示学习直觉，断裂的是系统闭环难度。

## 九、伦理与双用途

高分辨率人体相关数据与可干预模型并存时，需同步治理。本集未展开处，读者应自行补安全框架。

transcript.md:
**Nathan Labenz:** Hello, and welcome back to the Cognitive Revolution! Today my guest is Alex Rives, formerly co-founder and Chief Scientist at Evolutionary Scale, makers of the ESM series of models, and currently Head of Science at Biohub, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative backed moonshot with the inspiring mission to cure or prevent all disease, which just announced a $1.8B expansion of the Virtual Biology Initiative, a data-generation effort that brings together the Department of Energy, the NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic, and Meta. I opened by asking Alex what "curing all disease" means to him, and if I should expect to live much longer than the standard human lifespan. Calling himself "a practical person" in response, Alex described, not immortality, but a world without cancer, without infectious disease, and without chronic or degenerative conditions. From there, we get Alex's perspective on why today's virtual cell models haven't revolutionized medicine. The heart of the issue, Alex explains, is that our ability to observe what matters in biology is still very limited by the measurement technology we have available, and that as a result, we simply don't have the quality of data needed to represent the fine-grained causal structure that models presumably would be very happy to learn. Better architectures built on clever inductive biases can make the most of scarce data, such as in the extremely thoughtful use of physics in AlphaFold style models, and we do see real progress in next-token modeling of the biological code, but the available data is failing to capture critical information about how cells and tissues work. It's on this basis that Biohub is investing heavily in data, by opening new modalities, as they did with laser phase plate, an advance in microscopy that is allowing scientists to begin to directly see how individual proteins and other macromolecules interact inside the cell, and also by systematically building cell atlases that link molecular and imaging datasets across hundreds of billions of cells, representing both healthy and diseased states. The goal, over the next few years, is to build an information theoretic model of the cell, which effectively encodes the physical programs that run life, starting with a transition function that takes a cell or tissue state and a set of inputs and predicts a distribution of cell states at the next timestamp, ultimately building toward what Alex calls "a world model of life." This, of course, would support the use case I always dream of, which is answering the question: how do I push a pathologic state back to a healthy one, or in other words, effectively treat disease? Along the way, Alex describes how the LLM training paradigm applies to biology, his vision for "RLVR for biology", with lab verification, reacts to my proposal for "a million Bryan Johnsons", and ponders whether biological and language latent spaces will become deeply fused or remain separated by tool-calls, noting that the things we most want to know about biology are "novel concepts for which we don't yet have words and names." Finally, I asked Alex how he tracks his own health. He answered that he's so focused on Biohub research that he barely thinks about it, which surprised me, until I considered that, if he and the Biohub team are successful in creating the data layer needed to train highly generalizable biofoundation models, a little bit of timely, relevant personal health context might indeed be … all you need. With that, I hope you enjoy this look ahead toward a world model of life, with Alex Rives, Head of Science at Biohub. Main Episode

**Nathan Labenz:** Alex Reeves, head of science at Biohub. Welcome to the cognitive revolution.

**Alex Rives:** Thank you. Great to be here, Nathan.

**Nathan Labenz:** Yeah. I'm excited for this conversation. So let's start with the big picture. Biohub has this grandiose mission, which I'm excited about, of curing all diseases Yes. Mean to you? Should I think of that as synonymous with another phrase people sometimes use as solving biology? Should I think of it as applying to aging? Should I... You know, are we living forever in your vision of the future? Like, how grand does this vision ultimately get?

**Alex Rives:** Yeah. That's a great question.

**Nathan Labenz:** How do

**Alex Rives:** we define this? Well, I I I think I'm a practical person. Right? So I think about, you know, kinda what what is gonna be possible, I think, in a realistic time frame. And I think, you know, a good place to set our sights is to say that, you know, what we wanna do is is really live in a world without disease. Like, what would that mean? That would mean, you know, a world where there's not cancer, a world where there's not infectious disease, a world where there is not chronic disease or degenerative disease or, you know, all all the kinds of inflictions that have afflictions that have have have been, you know, really fundamental to to the human condition for a very long time. And, you know, I I think about that from a fundamental standpoint, like, you know, how do we how do we build the science that will, you know, really give us an understanding of of biology at a very deep and fundamental level that will under... Allow us to understand how disease works, that will allow us to to really identify the core mechanisms that will allow us to understand how how to detect disease, how to how how to how to intervene appropriately, and also kind of the the the technology. Right? So how can we go beyond kind of the current medical paradigm, which is, you know, kind of... And and I guess the therapeutic paradigm of of of kind of pills of of of molecules? You know, can we really go beyond that to far more programmable medicines that will will allow us to to really get to to the fundamentals of disease and really start to think about that as as as being able to to read and write the the programs of biology.

**Nathan Labenz:** So sometimes when I've thought about this in the past, I've tried to break this grand challenge down into two slightly less grand challenges. One of them is just understanding the causal structure of what's going on inside our bodies so that we could know what leads to problems and therefore what our targets for intervention should be. And then the other one is like having identified a target, figuring out something that can actually have the desired effect. How would you... Know, is that a good taxonomy? How would you break that taxonomy of challenges down further if you want to? And which ones do we have kind of the most traction on, and and where do we need to catch up?

**Alex Rives:** I mean, I think that's really the classic framework of drug development. So if you kind of think about, you know, how we think about creating a drug today, You know, we we think about physiology and disease. We try to identify really kind of a cause at the molecular level because that's where we can actually intervene today with the technology that we have. And then we really think about that problem of kind of, you know, finding and designing the intervention. And so, you know, that... That's that's kind of, I think, one paradigm. And I I think, you know, there's a there's a lot of progress that's that's still possible in that paradigm. So, you know, I I think that's that's kinda where we are today, of course. And and I think AI, you know, is is is is giving us, I think, really new potential to kind of look at each of the each of the parts of solving the... When you break the problem down that way, kind of each of the parts of solving it from that standpoint. But, I mean, I I think there's there's kind of also this this kind of, you know, more, I guess, like, information theoretic view on it that you might take where you can you can kind of think about, you know, life as as a program. Right? You can think about cells as as building living organisms, and you can really think about, you know, that that is a system of of rules, of code. And and you can think about, you know, what what what are the programs. Right? And, like, you know, how how do we... How could we read those programs? How could we start to start to rewrite those programs? And I think, you know, kind of thinking in in that way opens up a a wider aperture to to solving these problems. And I think a big part of kind of where we're trying to get with Biohub is is to really, you know, think about biology in that way, kind of create the tools for programmable biology, create the models that will allow us to understand biology in that context, you know, to really really start to understand how the cell works, both both both down to the molecular level, but also, you know, kinda kinda zooming out the cell in context and the the the, you know, the programs that that it runs to to build a living organism. And I think, you know, you could... You can really think as... Of disease as kind of a part of that. Right? It's it's really a part of the program. And and and if you think about it, you know, disease often unfolds in in very regular ways. So if we could kind of really understand that, I think it gives us really fundamentally new new tools to think about how how to make progress.

**Nathan Labenz:** So I know you guys are working toward virtual cell models. Of course, there have been virtual cell models for a while. My general understanding of the state of play right now is, like, they don't work super well largely, and people have kind of said... Or, you know, have advanced different hypotheses, I guess, let's say, for why that would be the case. The one that I have found the most compelling is basically the data we have is just not that high of quality such that it may not contain the signals that the ML models would really need to learn what's really going on. How would you react to that hypothesis? Like, where where do you think the... Everything that's happened so far, like, why hasn't it taken us further than it has today?

**Alex Rives:** Yeah. The, you know, the cell is incredibly complex. So I think I think you have to start there. You know? It's it's it's it's kind of like the right maybe meso scale for thinking about biology. But, you know, if you if you think about the cell, it's it's it's constituted by this just incredibly complex dynamic collection of of of matter, you know, where where kind of down to the level of individual atoms and and and and the interactions between between molecules. You know, those are those are... Those events are are determining of of of what happens at this... The the larger scale of the cell. And so... And and then... So so there's that kind of perspective, you know, building up from from, you know, the atomic resolution, kind of the first physical and chemical first principles. And then you can also kind of then think about the cell as as embedded within within, you know, living system, right, within within tissue, within physiology, within an organism, and sort of the complex programs that cells are able to execute to sense and respond to their environment, to communicate with each other, to, you know, really do these incredibly complicated and dynamic things. And so it's it's an immense immense challenge. And I think there are, you know, a number a number of limitations. So so so one is kind of, I think, you know, the models themselves, right, and just kind of having the right the right modeling approach and the right modeling paradigm. And, you know, we we have the transformer in in other areas of of AI, but the transformer kind of doesn't have that kind of multiscale structure that could could could represent those those different levels of of complexity. So there's there's kind of a question of of what's the right modeling paradigm. But then I think even more fundamental, there's the the question of of observation, observability, and measurement. And, you know, so much about the cell, you know, we just really can't measure. Sometimes we can't see it at all, And in many cases, kind of generating data at at scale would be really hard. And so if you you think about kind of many of the advances in science and biology, you know, they they really come from kind of having a new technology that that, you know, that that changes what we can measure, what we can observe. You know, the the the new powers to to to to see and observe biology, you know, can can really open up a new understanding of it. And so I I really think there's kind of three parts to really solving this problem. There's there's the modeling part. There's the there's the the the part of generating data at scale that's going to really reveal the the information architecture and the programs of the cell in in its in its kind of statistical structure. And then it's really, you know, the tools that we have to actually observe the cell and and and actually measure the things that that that matter. And I think you need to see progress on all three of those. And so, you know, the models that are being called virtual cells today, you know, I I just... I don't I don't think they meet that that definition of a model that that could actually simulate the cell in a meaningful way and actually really serve as an oracle for experimental biology.

**Nathan Labenz:** Let's do one more beat on how you imagine modeling evolving. I guess my naive sort of outside view, just based on all the success that we've seen in AI and language modeling and otherwise, is just like, if we had enough good data, feels to me like today's techniques would probably work. Maybe you would disagree with that. If you would disagree with that, what sort of future model do you envision? How do you think we sort of encode the right inductive priors and and sort of how how much of a, like, actual Rube Goldberg machine is the model? Is it, like, trying to match up the actual cell with, like, all the little proteins bopping around and interacting with each other and modeling all those, like, microstates? Or, you know, a kind of naive black box thing would be like, I have a cell. I perturb it. Like, what's the next state? You know, kind of the more of an input output without worrying about all the the detailed mechanisms inside. Where do you think we land on modeling when this really starts to work?

**Alex Rives:** Yeah. That's a that's a great question. So I should start by saying that, you know, I really think that kind of in the limit of, you know, data and can... The limit of infinite data and and compute, if you're thinking in limits, kind of all mark... Model architectures probably kinda end up being being the same. Right? They're just kind of function approximators. Right? And so if you have the right inputs and the outputs and you, you know, you learn a very, very good general function approximator, then then then in that sense and those limits, kind of the model architecture itself falls away. But I think I think in biology, you know, we're we're very far from that point. We're very far with some exceptions. Right? Like, with with protein biology, you know, we have gene sequencing at scale. You know, we really can kind of, you know, get closer and closer to kind of that limit of of of of infinite data. But for for cellular biology, you know, we're we're just so far from that right now. And I think historically, when you're far from that limit, you know, inductive bias becomes really important. turns.speaker: Nathan Labenz
turns.text: Hello, and welcome back to the Cognitive Revolution! Today my guest is Alex Rives, formerly co-founder and Chief Scientist at Evolutionary Scale, makers of the ESM series of models, and currently Head of Science at Biohub, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative backed moonshot with the inspiring mission to cure or prevent all disease, which just announced a $1.8B expansion of the Virtual Biology Initiative, a data-generation effort that brings together the Department of Energy, the NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic, and Meta. I opened by asking Alex what "curing all disease" means to him, and if I should expect to live much longer than the standard human lifespan. Calling himself "a practical person" in response, Alex described, not immortality, but a world without cancer, without infectious disease, and without chronic or degenerative conditions. From there, we get Alex's perspective on why today's virtual cell models haven't revolutionized medicine. The heart of the issue, Alex explains, is that our ability to observe what matters in biology is still very limited by the measurement technology we have available, and that as a result, we simply don't have the quality of data needed to represent the fine-grained causal structure that models presumably would be very happy to learn. Better architectures built on clever inductive biases can make the most of scarce data, such as in the extremely thoughtful use of physics in AlphaFold style models, and we do see real progress in next-token modeling of the biological code, but the available data is failing to capture critical information about how cells and tissues work. It's on this basis that Biohub is investing heavily in data, by opening new modalities, as they did with laser phase plate, an advance in microscopy that is allowing scientists to begin to directly see how individual proteins and other macromolecules interact inside the cell, and also by systematically building cell atlases that link molecular and imaging datasets across hundreds of billions of cells, representing both healthy and diseased states. The goal, over the next few years, is to build an information theoretic model of the cell, which effectively encodes the physical programs that run life, starting with a transition function that takes a cell or tissue state and a set of inputs and predicts a distribution of cell states at the next timestamp, ultimately building toward what Alex calls "a world model of life." This, of course, would support the use case I always dream of, which is answering the question: how do I push a pathologic state back to a healthy one, or in other words, effectively treat disease? Along the way, Alex describes how the LLM training paradigm applies to biology, his vision for "RLVR for biology", with lab verification, reacts to my proposal for "a million Bryan Johnsons", and ponders whether biological and language latent spaces will become deeply fused or remain separated by tool-calls, noting that the things we most want to know about biology are "novel concepts for which we don't yet have words and names." Finally, I asked Alex how he tracks his own health. He answered that he's so focused on Biohub research that he barely thinks about it, which surprised me, until I considered that, if he and the Biohub team are successful in creating the data layer needed to train highly generalizable biofoundation models, a little bit of timely, relevant personal health context might indeed be … all you need. With that, I hope you enjoy this look ahead toward a world model of life, with Alex Rives, Head of Science at Biohub. Main Episode
